passage.text: The teenagers below all want to attend a summer camp. Decide which summer camp would be the most suitable for each person.

passage.label: A
passage.text: Mountain Adventure Camp – A week of hiking, climbing, and camping in the hills. Learn outdoor survival skills, build campfires, and sleep in tents. Suitable for beginners. All equipment included. Arrival on Sunday.

passage.label: B
passage.text: Creative Arts Camp – A two-week programme focusing on painting, sculpture, and photography. Work with professional artists and create your own exhibition at the end of the camp. Materials provided. Suitable for all skill levels.

passage.label: C
passage.text: Science Discovery Camp – Explore biology, chemistry, and physics through exciting experiments. Build models and conduct field research in the local nature reserve. Small groups with expert tutors. Daily sessions from Monday to Friday.

passage.label: D
passage.text: Sports Performance Camp – Intensive training in athletics, swimming, and team sports. Improve your fitness and competition skills. Coaching from experienced trainers. Suitable for active teenagers. One-week programme.

passage.label: E
passage.text: Language Immersion Camp – Spend four weeks improving your French or Spanish with native speakers. Attend classes in the morning and take part in cultural activities in the afternoon. Homestay accommodation included.

passage.label: F
passage.text: Wildlife Conservation Camp – Help protect local wildlife by tracking animals, monitoring habitats, and planting trees. Work outdoors in the forest. One-week programme with camping. Ideal for nature lovers who enjoy working as a team.

passage.label: G
passage.text: Coding and Tech Camp – Learn to create your own video games, apps, and websites. Perfect for beginners who want to develop digital skills. Small groups with expert mentors. Bring your own laptop if possible. Two-week programme.

passage.label: H
passage.text: Music Performance Camp – Develop your singing or instrumental skills through daily rehearsals and concerts. Work with professional musicians. Open to all levels. Final concert for family and friends. One-week programme.

questionGroups.instruction: For each person, choose the most suitable summer camp. Write the correct letter A–H.

parts.passageTitle: Part 3 - Learning to Cook Under Pressure

passage.text: Learning to Cook Under Pressure

At sixteen, I was certain that becoming a chef meant inventing beautiful dishes and hearing customers praise them. I spent hours watching cooking programmes, but I had never worked in a professional kitchen. Before applying to college, I volunteered at a community cafe for six Saturdays. I expected to create exciting meals; instead, I chopped onions, washed pans and labelled containers. The work was repetitive, yet I enjoyed the speed and teamwork. More importantly, I discovered that I still wanted the job when nobody was watching or congratulating me.

The following year, I joined a catering course in Manchester. Our teacher, Mrs Khan, rarely criticised the taste of my food. She focused on everything surrounding it: whether I had prepared my equipment, avoided waste and cleaned as I worked. At first, this seemed unfair. Surely flavour mattered most? Then our class had to serve lunch to sixty guests. My soup tasted good, but I had forgotten to heat enough bowls, so several people received cold food. I finally understood that professional cooking depends as much on planning as on imagination.

During the summer, I found a position in a busy hotel. My first weeks were hardly glamorous. I arrived before sunrise to check deliveries and spent most evenings preparing vegetables. One night, another assistant became ill just before a wedding dinner. I was asked to take responsibility for the starters. I felt terrified, but I wrote a simple timetable and asked two colleagues to check it. Every plate left the kitchen on time. The head chef did not offer dramatic praise; she simply said, "You stayed calm and used the team." That quiet comment meant more to me than a round of applause.

Not every lesson was comfortable. I once copied an experienced chef's complicated dessert because I wanted to impress him. It looked perfect but tasted far too sweet. He told me that borrowing techniques was useful, while copying someone else's decisions was not. After that, I began testing simpler recipes and asking customers what they actually enjoyed. Some experiments failed, but each failure gave me information I could use.

I now work in a small restaurant where the menu changes with the seasons. I am still learning, and I no longer believe confidence means knowing every answer. For me, it means preparing carefully, listening to other people and recovering when a plan goes wrong. Television first attracted me to cooking, but ordinary tasks, honest feedback and unexpected pressure taught me how to become a chef.

parts.passageTitle: Part 5 — Learning to Cook Under Pressure

passage.text: Learning to Cook Under Pressure

When Maya first worked in a busy kitchen, she found the speed rather (21) ........ . Orders arrived constantly, and she had to (22) ........ several jobs at once. Her trainer told her to stay calm and (23) ........ attention to each instruction. At the beginning, Maya wrote short notes beside every order and checked them before passing a plate to the dining room. She sometimes felt nervous when three customers asked for changes at the same time, but the other cooks showed her how to divide the work. After a few weeks, Maya began to (24) ........ confidence and could organise her work more effectively. She also learned to (25) ........ mistakes quickly instead of hiding them. By the end of the season, she understood that a busy kitchen is not only about speed. It is about listening, helping colleagues and keeping a clear plan. This experience taught her that good cooking depends as much on teamwork (26) ........ it does on technical skill.

passage.text: Planning a Wildlife Walk

A wildlife walk is more enjoyable when you prepare carefully. Before setting out, check (27) ........ the path is open and tell someone where you are going. Take a map (28) ........ a fully charged phone, because weather can change quickly and some paths have poor signal. Wear comfortable clothes and carry water, even if the walk is short. You should walk quietly (29) ........ you do not frighten the animals. If the ground is wet, wear boots (30) ........ have a good grip. Stop often to look and listen instead of rushing from one place to another. Keep food in a sealed bag, and take all your rubbish (31) ........ you when you leave. Never follow an animal or try to touch it. Most importantly, remember (32) ........ watch from a safe distance. Good planning protects both visitors and wildlife.
